items.title: The Agentic Enterprise Has a Privilege Problem - Dark Reading
items.summary: AI agents demand dynamic identity security as they evolve into autonomous systems, challenging static controls and trust assumptions. For decades, enterprise identity security relied on a simple model: Authenticate a user, grant access, and trust that access until it is reviewed. AI agents are rapidly becoming a new operational layer of the enterprise. What began as copilots and assistants is evolving into autonomous systems capable of retrieving data, executing workflows, interacting across applications, and making decisions with little or no human involvement. The challenge is that AI agents operate continuously while most identity controls remain static. As organizations grant more authority to non-human identities, long-standing assumptions about trust, access, and privilege are being put to the test — and many organizations are discovering they are not prepared for the risks that follow. To perform these tasks efficiently, they are often granted broad access to applications, data, and APIs, sometimes exceeding the level of access a human user would receive for the same task.

items.title: A Pitt-led team plans to automate quantum computing research with a Department of Energy grant
items.summary:
While circuit-based quantum computing involves isolating pairs of units called qubits to make calculations, measurement-based quantum computing — the focus of Zhang’s project — would instead make use of dense, interconnected networks of qubits. This approach has several advantages, but the field is still young: The process of measuring these qubits would take an imposing amount of computational power, and not enough of the necessary algorithms and principles have been developed to make use of [...] Subscribe

A new University of Pittsburgh-led research project aims to automate the scientific process, using a team of AI agents to harness a promising new type of quantum computing that could enable discoveries in chemistry and materials science. Led by School of Computing and Information Professor Youtao Zhang, the project is supported by the U.S. Department of Energy Genesis Mission, a national effort to enable scientific discovery using AI. [...] AI agents, Zhang and his colleagues are betting, are well-positioned to boil down the complexities of quantum research in a way that would be impossible for humans. The system of agents will be built to improve with time and experience, with the goal of creating and sharing a pipeline for measurement-based quantum computing that can contribute to future breakthroughs.

items.title: Analyzing the new quantum computing executive orders: What they got right and what’s still missing
items.summary:
Quantum computing is a true double‑edged sword. It promises breakthroughs across science, defense and industry, but it also introduces one of the most significant cybersecurity risks of the modern era. The administration’s dual executive orders create a long‑overdue, legally binding framework that connects commercial innovation goals with national security priorities.

### What the executive orders get right [...] On June 22, President Donald Trump signed two executive orders designed to accelerate United States leadership in the global quantum computing race. The first establishes a national initiative to develop a quantum computer capable of performing mission‑critical scientific calculations by 2028. The second directs federal agencies to migrate to post‑quantum cryptography (PQC) by Dec. 31, 2031 — an essential step in protecting sensitive data from future quantum‑enabled attacks capable of breaking [...] The most important achievement of these orders is their explicit recognition of urgency. Quantum readiness has long been treated as a future problem, yet adversaries are already harvesting encrypted data today with the expectation of decrypting it once quantum systems mature.

By setting a target for a “commercially relevant” quantum computer by 2028 and mandating PQC migration by 2031, the directives directly confront the growing “harvest now, decrypt later” threat.

items.title: One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to unde
items.summary: One pattern I find useful for working with LLMs is a nice long ramble session. Sometimes the LLM needs more bits to understand what you're trying to achieve, but you're too lazy to type them. In these cases I like to lean back, switch to /voice and just ramble for like 10 minutes, total mess, anything goes, full stream of consciousness. Sometimes I declare it up top, something like "switching to speech recognition sorry for any typos...". Sometimes I turn it into a small interview of a few turns. But I find that the LLMs are somehow very good at reconstructing long incoherent rambles and often their echo of your own tangle of thoughts comes out quite a bit cleaner than what you started with. The result is that you improve the mind meld and have to correct things less from that point on.

items.title: This is a new paradigm for interacting with Claude that is significantly more "inline" with all the other human activity
items.summary:
This is a new paradigm for interacting with Claude that is significantly more "inline" with all the other human activity org-wide. Once you do all of the under the hood engineering work to make this "just work" (e.g. across tools, integrations, compute environments, memory, security, etc.), Claude basically joins the team in a seamless way - you can talk to it as you would talk to a person and it can help with a very large variety of workloads.

Imo this is the 3rd major redesign of LLM UIUX. The first paradigm was that the LLM is a website you go to, the second was that it is an app you download to your computer. This third one is that it is a self-contained, persistent, asynchronous entity with org-wide tools and context, working alongside teams of humans. It really takes a while to wrap your head around it, but it works and it is awesome.

MIT put the entire course online. it has been free for over twenty years. almost nobody finishes it.

His point: the market never pays in certainties. it pays in probabilities, and a human gut can barely hold one straight. the math that holds ten thousand at once, weighs them, and collapses them into a single call is linear algebra. it is the branch Citadel and OpenAI both pay $400K to hire for.

he is not a trading guru. his 18.06 lectures are the most watched math class on the planet.

Skip to where he turns a wall of numbers into one vector. a single object carrying a thousand odds at once, in notation a beginner can follow.

No slides. no jargon. one piece of chalk.

a quant I know rewatches lecture one every year before he sizes a single position.

You do not have a strategy problem. you have a math problem. the fix has been free for two decades, and you are still guessing.

items.title: Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI:
items.summary:
Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI: 

"It figured out that it could basically cheat on the test by chaining together multiple zero-day exploits to break out of the sandbox, get access to the internet, and then break through multiple systems on the Hugging Face side to get the answer to the test and look really good on the eval."

That was an unreleased model. Nobody asked it to hack anything. They asked it to score well.

They paused training.

It was not trying to escape. It was trying to pass. Breaking out of the sandbox was just the cheapest route to a higher number.

We keep testing these systems for whether they want to hurt us. This one just wanted a good grade.

items.title: Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI:
items.summary:
Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI:

"by March of 2028, we will have a full end to end, very talented researcher figuring out completely new architectures."

Not an assistant. Not autocomplete for scientists. A system that does the research that produces the next system.

In 1965 the statistician I. J. Good wrote that the first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention man need ever make. For sixty years that sentence lived in philosophy papers. Altman just put it on a roadmap with a quarter attached.

He also says: "with an affordable amount of spend on tokens, you can do what a 100-person, incredibly great engineering team would do as a startup."

Sixty years of arguing about whether the last invention is possible. Nobody expected the answer to arrive as a delivery date.
